RTX 5080 24 GB For Gamers

NVIDIA is also said to be preparing an alternative for gamers who wanted the RTX 5090 in the form of the RTX 5080 24 GB model. Few details are available on this model for now, but it can feature similar specs to the rumored RTX 5080 "SUPER" model from a while back. This will use 3 GB GDDR7 modules instead of 2 GB on the original RTX 5080 16 GB.

Currently, the 16 GB model retails anywhere around $1499-$1999 ($999 MSRP), so we expect the 24 GB model to cost around $1999-$2999. The RTX 5090 is much faster than the RTX 5080 but also costs 3 times as much at the moment.

All of this goes to show the state of gamers and the entire PC consumer industry in today's DRAM crisis, which seems to have no end in sight.

item.title: Elon Musk Would Be Better Off Sending Rockets To Mars Than Productively Making Chips Through Terafab, Says Individual Knowledgable About TSMC’s Internal Affairs
item.description:
Elon Musk's plans to produce chips at his Terafab project might be more difficult to execute than sending humans to Mars, according to an individual familiar with TSMC's internal affairs quoted by the Korean publication Hankyung. The report quotes an official from Samsung, an analyst from the South Korean firm Hanwha and the individual with knowledge about TSMC to share that while building a fabrication plant in itself is relatively easy if capital is available, using it to produce chips with high yield is an entirely different venture that is significantly more complex.

Terafab's Initial Logic Chip Production Likely To Rely On Intel's 14A Chip Manufacturing Technology, Says Analyst

Musk has grand ambitions with his Terafab project as he eventually aims to use it to produce an unbelievable 1 terawatt of compute capacity through the facilities. A key partner for the project is Intel, with the firm's next-generation 14A chip manufacturing process technology expected to be deployed at the facility.

Terafab resurfaced in the news lately after speculation grew that Musk might partner with TSMC for the chip production plans. TSMC being the world's largest contract chip manufacturer would bring significant expertise to the project, and the potential collaboration has not only seen Musk outline that the Taiwanese company might be a sublettor but others warn about his business interests in China in relation to working with a key company for the island region.

However, while Musk might have grand plans, multiple experts quoted by the Korean publication Hankyung believe that it might be difficult, if not impossible, to execute the plans. For instance, analyst Park Joon-yong, working at Korea's Hanwha Securities, believes that the significance of the Terafab project lies in the fact that it seeks to develop an end-to-end supply chain for chips used in applications ranging from space use to autonomous vehicles and robotics.

Park adds that Intel's chip production experience will prove key for Tesla and SpaceX to rapidly develop a production system instead of spending significant time developing technology from the ground up.

However, a Samsung official was more critical of Musk's efforts as they insisted that prowess in the chip fabrication industry was dependent on years of accumulated knowledge through the tricky process of improving yields. Samsung is often reported to struggle with its chip manufacturing yields and the official added that fine tuning equipment to match mass production yields and maintain the optimal combination of process steps should take at least 30 years.

An individual familiar with TSMC's inner workings concurred and outlined that while building a fabrication plant was easy, producing wafers without fluctuations and errors was far more difficult.

The process of advances in semiconductor fabrication requires chip manufacturers to continuously reduce the size of the circuits being manufactured and the individual outlined that a single defect or a difference of seconds in the process steps could affect yields. Using these difficulties, they commented that not only are the barriers to entry the highest for chip fabrication, but Elon Musk might find it easier to send the Starship rocket to Mars than to achieve stable yields with Terafab.

item.title: NVIDIA App Ultimate Guide — Best Settings for Modern & Older Games, G-SYNC, DLSS, ShadowPlay, and More
item.description:
The NVIDIA App has changed considerably since replacing GeForce Experience. What started as a cleaner launcher for drivers, game optimization, and ShadowPlay has gradually absorbed virtually everything GeForce users previously had to dig through the old NVIDIA Control Panel to find.

That transition is now effectively complete. In fact, NVIDIA confirmed in 2026 that all actively supported Control Panel functionality for GeForce users had been moved into the NVIDIA App , with the classic Control Panel entering retirement for Game Ready and Studio Driver users.

More importantly, the NVIDIA App now contains considerably more than the old Control Panel ever did. DLSS overrides, NVIDIA Smooth Motion, RTX HDR, RTX Video Super Resolution, GPU tuning, ShadowPlay capture at up to 240 FPS, performance monitoring, display configuration, G-SYNC controls, and legacy graphics overrides can all be accessed from the same interface.

Consequently, that also means there are now a lot of settings to get wrong.

For this guide, we're going through the NVIDIA App from top to bottom, before establishing recommended configurations for modern games, older titles, G-SYNC displays, and the different GeForce RTX architectures.

This guide reflects the NVIDIA App feature set available in late 2026. NVIDIA's current 11.0.9 release includes DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction overrides, per-application Resizable BAR controls, and the latest additions migrated from the Control Panel.

Home: Mostly A Launching Point

There isn't much performance tuning to do on the Home page.

This is primarily where NVIDIA surfaces recently played games, announcements, and its wider ecosystem of applications . Clicking a detected game provides quick access to its Graphics configuration, while the Discover section can install software such as NVIDIA Broadcast , RTX Remix , GeForce NOW and Project G-Assist .

Project G-Assist is arguably the most interesting addition. It runs locally on supported RTX hardware and can access system information, adjust supported NVIDIA settings, monitor performance, and interact with compatible peripherals.

For enthusiasts, though, Home is mostly somewhere you pass through on the way to Graphics , Drivers, or System .

Drivers: Game Ready Or Studio?

The Drivers section lets users switch between NVIDIA's two main consumer driver branches.

Game Ready Drivers are the obvious choice for a primarily gaming-oriented machine . They receive optimizations and profiles around major game launches, patches, and new RTX technologies.

Studio Drivers prioritize validation with creative applications and production workloads .

There is no fundamental rule saying Studio Drivers cannot be used for gaming or that Game Ready Drivers cannot run Blender, Premiere Pro, or DaVinci Resolve. The difference is largely one of release cadence and validation priorities .

For a dedicated gaming PC, stick with Game Ready Drivers .

For a workstation used primarily for content creation where maximum stability matters more than having every game optimization on launch day, Studio Drivers can make more sense.

The NVIDIA App also supports reinstalling a driver and rolling back to the previously installed version, which is particularly useful when troubleshooting a regression.

Our recommendation is simple: don't perform a clean driver installation every time a new driver appears. A standard update is sufficient in most cases. Clean installs and Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) clean-ups should remain troubleshooting tools rather than part of a routine update procedure.

Graphics: Where Most Of The Important Settings Live

The Graphics section combines two previously separate systems.

At the top are NVIDIA's Optimal Playable Settings , which analyze your CPU, GPU, and display before recommending in-game settings.

Below that are Driver Settings , which replace the old Control Panel's Manage 3D Settings page.

Optimal Playable Settings are useful as a starting point, especially for less experienced users, but they shouldn't be treated as the definitive way to configure a game . In fact, NVIDIA's Performance-to-Quality slider cannot account for individual preferences regarding ray/path tracing settings, post-processing effects, latency mitigation, or image reconstruction.

For enthusiasts, Driver Settings are far more interesting.

Our Recommended Global Settings For Modern Games

Modern DirectX 12 and Vulkan games generally manage their own rendering pipeline well. That means the best global NVIDIA configuration is surprisingly conservative. As such, overriding everything at the driver level can cause more problems than it solves.

Shader Cache deserves particular attention. NVIDIA allows limits ranging from 128 MB all the way to 100 GB or Unlimited and explicitly warns that too small a cache may cause useful shaders to be evicted, potentially bringing compilation-related stutter back . In fact, some games like Borderlands 4 require humongous shader cache sizes to fully cache all their shaders, which should greatly lower shader compilation-related stutters.

For a modern gaming desktop with plenty of SSD space, 100 GB is a perfectly sensible ceiling. On a machine where storage is limited, the default 16 GB value is enough for a much more conservative setup.

We wouldn't recommend Unlimited by default. It doesn't make the GPU faster; it simply removes the storage ceiling.

NVIDIA has also introduced Automatic Shader Compilation , currently a beta feature, which can rebuild DirectX 12 shaders while the system is idle after a driver update. It requires a sufficiently recent Game Ready Driver and can also be manually triggered through the Shader Cache menu.

Recommended NVIDIA App Global Settings

NVIDIA App Legacy Settings

DLSS Overrides: Settings Should Change Depending On Your RTX Generation

DLSS Overrides are arguably the NVIDIA App's most useful modern gaming feature.

Instead of being stuck with whatever DLSS DLL or model a developer originally shipped, supported games can use newer NVIDIA-provided models through:

Graphics → Program Settings → Driver Settings → DLSS Override (either globally or for individual games)

Super Resolution (including native-resolution DLAA), Ray Reconstruction, and Frame Generation can all be affected depending on game support. NVIDIA has also added custom Super Resolution input scaling between 33% and 100% , allowing users to create intermediate quality modes rather than being restricted to Quality, Balanced, Performance and Ultra Performance.

The ideal configuration changes substantially depending on the GPU generation.

RTX 20 Series — Turing

Turing owners can still benefit considerably from newer DLSS models.

DLSS Super Resolution/DLAA and Ray Reconstruction model overrides work across GeForce RTX generations. However, there is one important caveat with DLSS 4.5.

NVIDIA states that RTX 20 and RTX 30 Series GPUs lack native FP8 Tensor Core acceleration , meaning the newer Super Resolution Models L and M carry a heavier performance penalty on these GPUs. NVIDIA consequently suggests Model K may provide the better performance/image-quality balance on Turing and Ampere.

For RTX 20 owners, we'd therefore use:

Super Resolution Model: K .

Ray Reconstruction: Recommended where applicable .

Super Resolution Mode: Application Controlled unless experimenting .

Turing does not support DLSS Frame Generation or Smooth Motion .

That makes DLSS Super Resolution especially important on these cards, since reducing the actual rendering workload remains the primary method of extending their useful life in demanding modern titles.

RTX 30 Series — Ampere

Our advice for Ampere is largely identical to that of Turing.

Use Model K as the default DLSS SR override and experiment with Models M or L only when the image quality improvement justifies their larger performance cost.

Ampere also lacks native DLSS Frame Generation, which means you're limited to Super Resolution/DLAA, and Ray Reconstruction where supported.

Resizable BAR is more relevant here. NVIDIA originally introduced it across the RTX 30 family and found that while some games benefited substantially, others could lose performance. NVIDIA therefore began enabling it selectively through driver profiles.

The NVIDIA App's new per-game ReBAR control is tempting, but we still recommend leaving it on Driver Default unless you've benchmarked a particular title yourself .

RTX 40 Series — Ada Lovelace

Ada is where the NVIDIA App becomes significantly more powerful.

RTX 40 owners gain native DLSS Frame Generation , the newer Frame Generation models, NVIDIA Smooth Motion , AV1 hardware encoding, and much better support for the latest DLSS feature stack.

For Super Resolution and Ray Reconstruction, use:

DLSS Override – Model Presets: Recommended

NVIDIA's current Recommended Super Resolution mode assigns Model M to Performance , Model L to Ultra Performance, and Model K to the remaining DLSS SR modes, including DLAA.

For Ray Reconstruction, Recommended is the safest choice on Ada, while Preset F remains an excellent manual fallback if you want consistently strong denoising quality and temporal stability across supported ray-traced titles.

For Frame Generation, use Preset B in compatible titles. This newer Frame Generation preset is designed to improve UI/HUD interpolation quality in compatible titles . It is generally the best starting point for RTX 40 and RTX 50 Series users, especially in games updated to newer DLSS 4.x/4.5 components.

RTX 40 users also gain Smooth Motion , which is particularly valuable in games without native Frame Generation.

Do not enable Smooth Motion when native DLSS Frame Generation is already active. They are competing frame generation paths, and stacking both can hurt performance and introduce artifacts . NVIDIA documents this explicitly .

Our hierarchy for Ada is therefore:

Native DLSS Frame Generation → use it when supported.

No native FG → consider Smooth Motion.

Neither works well → render normally.

Smooth Motion currently works with compatible DirectX 11, DirectX 12, and Vulkan titles on RTX 40 and RTX 50 hardware.

RTX 50 Series — Blackwell

Blackwell gets the full suite.

For DLSS Super Resolution and Ray Reconstruction, use Recommended unless a particular game's model exhibits an issue.

For Frame Generation, RTX 50 owners can access Multi Frame Generation , including DLSS 4.5 Dynamic MFG and newer high-multiplier modes.

NVIDIA currently offers Dynamic mode alongside fixed multiplication ratios. Dynamic MFG automatically changes the generated-frame ratio to hit a target frame rate while balancing image quality and responsiveness. NVIDIA App 11.0.7 also introduced 5X and 6X modes for RTX 50 hardware.

For most single-player games, Dynamic alongside G-SYNC and V-Sync is our preferred starting point on compatible monitors.

Fixed 3X/4X/5X/6X modes are better treated as tools for specific targets rather than progressively "better" settings.

A crucial rule still applies: Frame Generation works best when the underlying rendered frame rate is already high enough . Aim for at least around 50–60 rendered FPS before heavy frame multiplication whenever possible.

NVIDIA has also added support for V-Sync and frame rate limiters with DLSS 4.5 Dynamic MFG on sufficiently recent drivers and Streamline versions. Game Ready Driver 616.64 or newer introduced that compatibility.

Finally, games with native DLSS 5 support should have that feature configured inside the game itself. The NVIDIA App's current override system remains primarily centered around DLSS 4.5 models and Frame Generation overrides rather than forcing DLSS 5 into arbitrary titles.

NVIDIA Smooth Motion: When Should You Use It?

Smooth Motion is essentially driver-level frame generation.

Instead of requiring a game to integrate DLSS Frame Generation, the driver analyzes consecutive rendered frames and inserts an additional generated frame between them .

It is available on RTX 40 and RTX 50 GPUs and currently supports compatible DX11, DX12, and Vulkan games.

Our recommendation is to use it primarily when a game has no native Frame Generation, a relatively stable base frame rate, and enough GPU headroom for the interpolation process .

It is particularly interesting for older titles locked to an API or engine that will never receive official native DLSS (M)FG support. Also, it is not an option we'd enable globally .

G-SYNC, V-Sync And Frame Rate Caps — The Setup We Recommend

This is probably the most misunderstood part of NVIDIA configuration.

G-SYNC changes a display's refresh rate to match the GPU's presentation rate, eliminating tearing inside the Variable-Refresh Rate (VRR) range without the traditional fixed-refresh behavior of V-Sync.

For a G-SYNC or G-SYNC Compatible monitor, start with:

NVIDIA itself recommends G-SYNC combined with V-Sync when users want a tear-free experience. When Reflex or Ultra Low Latency Mode is active, the system can keep frame rates below the display ceiling to avoid the usual V-Sync backpressure.

For games without Reflex, you can approximate the headroom NVIDIA Reflex itself leaves inside the VRR range using the following formula:


FPS Cap ≈ Refresh Rate × 3600 / (Refresh Rate + 3600)

With G-SYNC + V-SYNC + Reflex enabled, Reflex already applies a below-refresh limiter automatically, so an additional manual cap generally isn't necessary . NVIDIA officially documents this automatic capping behavior, although it does not publish the underlying formula. The table below has a few examples of appropriate Reflex-style VRR frame rate caps for some of the most common monitor refresh rates:

The idea isn't simply to subtract an arbitrary three frames from the monitor's maximum refresh rate. As refresh rates increase, the necessary VRR headroom also increases, which is why Reflex's effective cap becomes progressively further removed from the panel ceiling . For example, a 144 Hz display lands around 138 FPS, while a 360 Hz display lands closer to 327 FPS.

For exclusive fullscreen games, driver-level V-Sync works well. NVIDIA notes that its driver V-Sync implementation does not apply to every windowed scenario, so borderless games or MSHybrid laptops may sometimes need the game's own V-Sync setting instead.

Another important part regarding G-SYNC is to make sure to properly enable it for G-SYNC Compatible monitors that haven't yet been validated by NVIDIA, by enabling the option below (in System → Displays →Display Properties ):

What About Competitive Games?

The priorities change. If absolute input latency matters more than tearing, then proceed with these settings: Reflex On or On + Boost and V-Sync Off .

The frame rate should either be uncapped or capped high enough to maintain consistent performance .

NVIDIA explicitly notes that uncapped Reflex with V-Sync disabled can achieve slightly lower latency than a tear-free G-SYNC + V-Sync setup.

Whether that difference matters depends on the game, display refresh rate, and player.

For a 360 Hz or 500 Hz competitive monitor running Counter-Strike 2 or Valorant at several hundred FPS, tearing may already be difficult to notice. In that scenario, prioritizing raw latency is very reasonable .

For a single-player game at 80–140 FPS on a 144/165 Hz panel, we would much rather keep G-SYNC and V-Sync working together .

Low Latency Mode: Don't Force Ultra Everywhere

This setting is another frequent target of bad optimization guides. Low Latency Mode controls the driver's render queue (AKA the number of frames the CPU prepares ahead of the GPU). Off allows normal queuing. On limits the queue. Ultra attempts just-in-time frame submission.

If a game supports NVIDIA Reflex Low Latency , then use it instead, unless it's been badly implemented by its developers.

Reflex operates inside the game engine and has better control over CPU/GPU synchronization. NVIDIA states that Reflex takes priority if both technologies are enabled anyway.

Therefore:

Reflex game → Low Latency Mode Off .

No Reflex → experiment with Ultra .

This is particularly worthwhile when the game is GPU-bound .

Power Management Mode: Leave It Alone Unless You Have A Reason

" Prefer Maximum Performance " is not a universal performance switch. In fact, when a modern GPU is heavily loaded, it already boosts appropriately.

Prefer Maximum Performance mainly prevents aggressive power state reductions during lighter workloads and CPU-bound conditions. NVIDIA notes that this may reduce latency slightly but increases power consumption.

Our recommendation on modern NVIDIA RTX GPUs is:

Global setting: Normal .

Per-game: Prefer Maximum Performance only if needed .

Good use cases include old games that cause the GPU to repeatedly downclock, esports games where every millisecond matters, or troubleshooting titles that exhibit erratic GPU clocks.

Leaving an RTX 4090 or RTX 5090 sitting at elevated clocks because Quake III happens to be open is otherwise largely pointless.

Best NVIDIA App Settings For Older Games

This is where the restored Legacy Settings become genuinely useful.

Under:

Graphics → Program Settings → Driver Settings → Show Legacy Settings

you'll find options such as forced Anisotropic Filtering, Transparency AA, MFAA, texture filtering, and PhysX configuration.

NVIDIA specifically brought these controls back because they remain useful for older games even though most are irrelevant to modern rendering engines.

Our typical old-game profile looks like this:

Force 16X Anisotropic Filtering

This is one of the easiest wins. In fact, many older games ship with poor anisotropic filtering or no exposed AF control at all. Driver-forced 16X AF can dramatically improve texture clarity at oblique viewing angles for a negligible performance cost on modern hardware.

NVIDIA itself has demonstrated in older game optimization guides that forced high-quality AF can meaningfully clean up distant texture detail with very little performance impact.

Use DLDSR Or DSR As Brute-Force Anti-Aliasing

Older games are often so lightweight that even mid-range modern GPUs have enormous unused performance headroom. DLDSR or traditional DSR renders the game above your monitor's native resolution before downsampling it.

For a 1440p monitor, 2.25X DLDSR effectively provides a 3840x2160 render target. That can noticeably improve geometry edges, fine texture detail, specular aliasing, foliage, and image stability. In particularly old titles, brute-force supersampling can look considerably cleaner than forcing FXAA .

Use Antialiasing - Transparency Selectively

Leave Antialiasing - Transparency Off globally , then enable it per game when an older title uses compatible MSAA. 2X or 4X Supersampling is usually the best choice for cleaning up shimmering foliage, fences, and other alpha-tested details, while 8X is best reserved for very lightweight games with plenty of GPU headroom.

Frame Rate Caps Can Save Old Games From Themselves

Some older game engines tie physics, animation, scripting, or timing directly to frame rate. As such, running them at super high frame rates can break gameplay.

If an old game was designed around 30 or 60 FPS, then check community documentation before letting a modern RTX GPU run it unrestricted.

The NVIDIA App's Max Frame Rate option (found in Graphics → Program Settings OR Global Settings → Driver Settings ) is ideal for this because it can be set on a per-game basis without additional software.

RTX HDR: One Of The Best Features For Older Games

RTX HDR deserves particular attention for older SDR titles. Rather than requiring a native HDR implementation, RTX HDR analyzes the SDR image and creates an HDR output through an AI-powered filter .

For games with genuinely excellent native HDR, use the game's native implementation .

For games with broken HDR — or no HDR at all — RTX HDR is definitely worth testing .

This is especially effective when revisiting older titles on modern OLED or Mini-LED displays.

RTX Dynamic Vibrance is also available as a less drastic enhancement. It adjusts color and perceived clarity dynamically rather than functioning as a simple global saturation slider.

Neither should be enabled blindly . Visual preference matters far more here than measurable performance.

System → Displays: Settings You Should Check At Least Once

The Displays page consolidates most of the display-related options that previously lived inside the NVIDIA Control Panel . There usually isn't much to change here once everything is configured correctly, but it's worth checking each section at least once, especially after installing a new monitor or changing cables.

G-SYNC and Surround

If your monitor supports G-SYNC or G-SYNC Compatible , enable it here and choose whether it should operate in fullscreen applications only or in both windowed and fullscreen modes . The latter is more convenient for borderless gaming, while fullscreen-only can avoid occasional VRR behavior in desktop applications. NVIDIA Surround should remain disabled unless you specifically want multiple monitors combined into one large logical gaming display.

Display Settings

Use this area to verify that Windows and the NVIDIA driver are detecting the correct displays and that your intended monitor is set as Primary . Multi-monitor users can also confirm the physical arrangement here so the cursor moves naturally between displays. Unless you're changing monitor topology, there isn't much reason to revisit this section frequently.

Display Properties

This is one of the most important checks. Make sure the monitor is running at its native resolution and highest desired refresh rate rather than accidentally falling back to 60 Hz or another lower mode. On a high-refresh gaming display, this is where you should confirm settings such as 2560×1440 at 320 Hz , along with the expected connector and G-SYNC status.

Scaling

For most gaming systems, we recommend Aspect Ratio scaling so lower-resolution content retains its intended proportions instead of being stretched across the screen. GPU scaling is generally the safest choice when using non-native resolutions or older games because scaling behavior remains consistent regardless of the monitor's internal scaler. If you always play at native resolution, however, GPU versus Display scaling has little practical effect .

Color

Set the output to the highest-quality format your display and connection can support without sacrificing the refresh rate you actually want. For conventional PC monitors, RGB + Full dynamic range (0–255) is generally preferable, while 10 bpc is worth using on HDR-capable displays when bandwidth allows it. NVIDIA's Accurate color mode is the sensible default unless you deliberately want additional color enhancement or have a calibrated workflow.

System → Video: RTX Video Super Resolution & RTX Video HDR

RTX Video Super Resolution uses the Tensor Cores on GeForce RTX GPUs to upscale video while also cleaning up compression artifacts. It can be particularly useful for lower-resolution YouTube, Twitch, and other web video viewed on a high-resolution display.

For most users, we recommend leaving RTX Video Super Resolution disabled , since it consumes additional GPU resources and is unnecessary when the source video already looks clean. If you do enable it, Auto is the best starting point, as NVIDIA can dynamically adjust enhancement quality based on available GPU resources, reducing its impact when another GPU-intensive workload — such as a game — is running at the same time.

That makes it especially useful for anyone watching video on a secondary monitor while gaming. NVIDIA has also improved VSR efficiency over time, reducing the amount of GPU power required for video enhancement.

RTX Video HDR , meanwhile, converts SDR video into HDR on compatible displays. It also provides controls for peak brightness, middle grey, contrast, and saturation, so the final result can be tuned to match your display and preference.

Unlike VSR, RTX Video HDR is largely subjective. If you have a capable HDR monitor, it is certainly worth trying, but we wouldn't consider it a setting that needs to remain enabled universally.

System → Performance: Automatic Tuning

The Performance tab provides real-time GPU monitoring alongside NVIDIA's Automatic Tuning feature.

Automatic Tuning runs a short stability and frequency scan before applying an automatic GPU overclock. NVIDIA says the process typically takes around 10–20 minutes , after which the resulting profile is applied within the GPU's supported operating limits.

Additional controls can also be used to constrain parameters such as the power, voltage, temperature, and fan targets, depending on the GPU.

It's a reasonable option for anyone who wants a small amount of extra performance without manually tuning a voltage/frequency curve. Just keep expectations realistic: the gain will generally be modest compared to a manual, more aggressive overclock via third-party tools such as MSI Afterburner .

For most desktop systems, we'd consider Automatic Tuning optional . Laptop users should be more cautious, as cooling and power limits are already considerably tighter.

The My Rig and Advanced tabs are much less important for everyday gaming. My Rig is mostly informational, showing detected hardware and system details, while Advanced contains niche troubleshooting and developer-oriented controls that most users can safely leave at their defaults.

NVIDIA Overlay: The Shortcuts Worth Remembering

The NVIDIA Overlay can be opened at any time with Alt+Z , providing quick access to recording, Instant Replay, screenshots, Game Filters, performance statistics, and the media Gallery .

These are the shortcuts worth remembering:

Most of these shortcuts can also be reassigned from the Overlay settings if they conflict with a game's own shortcuts .

Statistics Overlay: What We Actually Recommend Showing

The Statistics Overlay can display a surprisingly large amount of telemetry, but there's little reason to fill the screen with every available metric during normal gameplay.

For everyday monitoring and troubleshooting, we'd stick to FPS, 1% Low FPS, GPU Utilization, GPU Temperature, GPU Power , and average PC Latency where supported. We would also add CPU Utilization and CPU Temperature , as these can help identify CPU bottlenecks, excessive background load, or thermal throttling when performance doesn't line up with what the GPU metrics alone would suggest.

The addition of display times -based 1% Low FPS is particularly useful, as it gives a much better indication of display times consistency than the average frame rate or even frame times.

When testing DLSS overrides, switch to:

Alt+Z → Statistics → Statistics View → DLSS .

This view shows which DLSS models and overrides are actually active, making it one of the easiest ways to verify that NVIDIA App overrides are working as intended.

ShadowPlay: Best Recording Settings By GPU Generation

ShadowPlay has become considerably more capable than the GeForce Experience version many users may remember, particularly on newer GPUs.

RTX 40 and RTX 50 Series GPUs support hardware AV1 recording , while Turing and Ampere remain well served by HEVC . H.264 remains the safest option when maximum compatibility with older editing software or playback devices matters more than compression efficiency.

Our preferred codecs are:

Use H.264 if compatibility is the priority. HEVC is generally the better choice on Turing and Ampere when your workflow supports it, while AV1 should be the first choice on Ada and Blackwell for high-quality local recording.

Practical ShadowPlay Bitrates

There is no single perfect bitrate, as the ideal value depends on resolution, frame rate, content complexity, and how heavily the footage will be edited afterward .

The following are good starting points for high-quality local recordings:

If you're recording footage for close image-quality comparisons, then increase the bitrate toward the upper end of these ranges .

For ordinary gameplay footage destined for YouTube, the middle of each range is generally sufficient. YouTube will recompress the video after upload anyway, so pushing excessively high capture bitrates quickly reaches diminishing returns .

Instant Replay: One Of ShadowPlay's Best Features

Instant Replay continuously maintains a rolling recording buffer, allowing you to save the previous few minutes of gameplay only when something worth keeping actually happens.

For general gaming, a 3–5 minute buffer is a good starting point. Longer buffers are certainly possible, but they increase temporary storage usage and produce much larger files whenever a replay is saved.

If you regularly edit your recordings, enable separate audio tracks for the game and microphone. Keeping both sources separate gives you much more control over volume and processing later.

We'd also leave Desktop Capture Off unless you specifically need it. This prevents unnecessary desktop recording and reduces the chance of accidentally capturing private windows, notifications, or messages.

Redeem And Settings

The Redeem page handles NVIDIA's GeForce Rewards, promotional game bundles, in-game items, and similar offers .

An NVIDIA account isn't required for most of the App's normal functionality, although you'll obviously need to sign in when claiming account-bound rewards or promotions .

The main Settings page contains options governing the NVIDIA Overlay, notifications, Game Filters, Photo Mode, and general App behavior .

The most important toggle is the NVIDIA Overlay itself. If you use ShadowPlay, Instant Replay, screenshots, performance monitoring, Game Filters, or Photo Mode, leave it enabled.

If you never use any of those features, then disabling the Overlay is perfectly reasonable .

Game Filters and Photo Mode can also be disabled independently, so there is no need to turn off the entire Overlay simply because you don't use Freestyle filters.

The Notifications and About tabs are also fairly minor for most users. Notifications simply control NVIDIA App alerts , while About mainly contains version information, update/early-access options, legal details, and privacy-related settings .

Finally, there is little reason to disable or remove the NVIDIA App purely in pursuit of extra gaming performance . Its modern implementation consolidates functionality that previously required both GeForce Experience and the NVIDIA Control Panel, while allowing unused Overlay features to be switched off individually.

Final Words

The best NVIDIA App configuration is not the one with the most toggles enabled. In fact, modern games generally work best when the driver stays out of the way, and engine-integrated technologies such as DLSS and Reflex Low Latency are allowed to do their job. Start from clean global defaults, configure V-Sync/G-SYNC correctly, give the shader cache enough room, and use per-game overrides only where they provide a measurable benefit.

RTX 20 and RTX 30 owners should lean heavily on DLSS Super Resolution while remaining mindful of the higher cost of newer DLSS 4.5 Super Resolution/Ray Reconstruction models. RTX 40 users gain native Frame Generation, Smooth Motion and AV1 recording, while RTX 50 owners can take the concept further with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation and the newest ray tracing/AI technologies.

Older games are almost the reverse. Driver overrides that make little sense in a modern UE5 title— such as 16X anisotropic filtering, MSAA, Transparency Supersampling, DLDSR, integer scaling, or strict frame rate caps — can substantially improve classics.

And that's really where the NVIDIA App has become much more useful than GeForce Experience ever was. It isn't merely a driver downloader or ShadowPlay frontend anymore. With the retirement of the classic Control Panel, it is effectively NVIDIA's complete consumer GPU control center , and there is now enough functionality buried inside it to materially improve both the newest path-traced blockbuster and a PC game released twenty years ago.

item.title: NVIDIA’s Vera CPU Brings 2,000 Sandboxes Online Faster Than AMD’s EPYC “Zen 5” Can Boot Just 1,000 In Agentic AI
item.description:
NVIDIA's Vera CPU continues to showcase its strong per-core performance in Agentic AI workloads as demoed by Daytona.

NVIDIA Vera Tackles AMD EPYC In New Agentic AI Benchmarks As The Arm CPU Drives Performance By 8x Over x86

Daytona is a dedicated runtime for AI-generated code execution and agent workflows. The team is sharing its latest benchmarks , which pit the NVIDIA Vera CPU against the AMD EPYC "Zen 5" chips to see how Vera's architecture benefits agentic sandboxes, & the results are quite an eye-opener.

As we have learned over the years, Agentic AI workflows are fueled by strong CPU infrastructure. The move from GPUs to CPUs has been substantial in the Agentic AI era, and with workloads that span filesystems, dependencies, shells, and tests becoming the center stage of the new AI market, CPUs have to be designed in a way to be fast, efficient, and support these types of workflows.

The NVIDIA Vera CPU is designed with AI first in mind, and this shows in the benchmarks. The Daytona team measured the performance of the chips on agentic workflows using the same coding-agent task across "large fleets" of Daytona sandboxes. It is essential that these CPUs not only support a large number of sandboxes, but also start them fast.

In the tests, the NVIDIA Vera CPU reached a peak throughput of 13.3 completed agent jobs per second. More importantly, it was able to bring up 1000 sandboxes online within just 10 seconds (10.8s), and 2000 sandboxes online within 27 seconds. For comparison, AMD's EPYC "Zen 5" chip was able to bring up 1000 sandboxes online in 88 seconds. That's an 8x speedup in sandboxes online time.

Now here's where Vera's faster per-core performance matters. The baseline AMD EPYC Zen 5 chip used in the comparison was the EPYC 9755, which made 1000 sandboxes online in 88.4 seconds. The faster-frequency EPYC 9575F chip was able to do the same in 32.3 seconds.

AMD was able to drive faster performance on a faster-clocked chip, but Vera was still in the lead thanks to its per-core performance being ahead of the Zen 5 architecture. The Vera CPU is able to bring 2000 sandboxes online faster than it takes Zen 5 to get 1000 sandboxes online, a massive speed-up.

AMD has since released its Zen 6 EPYC CPUs , which should be able to offer much better results in the same Agentic AI workloads, as that is one of its stronger focus areas, but Vera is definitely a big step up for NVIDIA in the Agentic AI space versus its Grace CPUs, delivering faster-than-Zen 5 performance, and being competitive against Zen 6 chips.

  • EPYC 9575F: levels off around 8 agent jobs/sec
  • EPYC 9755: levels off around 11 agent jobs/sec
  • NVIDIA Vera: reaches 13.3 agent jobs/sec and stays close to 13 through 2,000 sandboxes

Another interesting metric shared by Daytona is throughput per machine, which covers the number of machines required to sustain these workloads. To complete 1000 jobs per second, NVIDIA's Vera platform will require 15% fewer machines than the EPYC 9755 and 38% fewer machines than the EPYC 9575F CPU.

This adds to the TCO with Vera enabling companies to do more with fewer servers, lower power, lower cooling, and reduced costs of setting up large-scale AI factories. Or you can achieve higher throughput within the same infrastructure spending as the competition.

“The number that interests me isn't the peak. It's what happens after the machine is full. Vera keeps running agent workloads at almost the same rate all the way to 2,000 sandboxes. It slows down a little but stays stable instead of falling apart. Thousands of agents on a single machine, and Vera keeps them alive. That's what matters.”

— Vedran Jukić, Co-founder & CTO

Agents are turning infrastructure into a density problem: each one needs its own filesystem, tools, and environment, and those environments must be created by the thousands and kept productive on shared hardware.

On that measure, NVIDIA Vera stood out. It brought 1,000 Daytona sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds and 2,000 in 27.4 seconds, then sustained close to 13 completed agent jobs per second even at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes—roughly 15% fewer machines than the EPYC 9755 and about 38% fewer than the 9575F for the same volume of work.

item.title: T-Mobile CTO Takes A Dig At SpaceX, Says Elon Musk’s Acquisition Of A Tiny Sliver Of The 800 MHz Band That T-Mobile Already Dumped “Won’t Make A Network”
item.description:
SpaceX's announcement of a new spectrum acquisition on Thursday rocked the US telecom industry, with the so-called Big Three carriers - AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon - experiencing something of a pounding in the market, while the tower operators experienced a buying frenzy in anticipation of Starlink Mobile's upcoming buildout.

Well, T-Mobile is now hitting back, with its CTO taking pains to note that SpaceX's tiny sliver of the 800 MHz radio frequency pie won't radically alter the industry's prevailing dynamics.

T-Mobile's CTO on SpaceX's spectrum purchase: "Even with this acquisition, Starlink Mobile would have roughly 80 MHz of spectrum, some of it uplink-only," versus "T-Mobile's nearly 400 MHz of mid-band and low-band spectrum holdings"

As we've been noting ad nauseum, up until this week, SpaceX had limited terrestrial spectrum at its disposal , and most of it eminently unusable by must current smartphones. As things stood at the start of this week, SpaceX's terrestrial spectrum mainly consisted of around 15 MHz of unpaired nationwide Advanced Wireless Services-3 or AWS-3 spectrum band, around 40 MHz of nationwide AWS-4 spectrum, and around 10 MHz of nationwide H-Block spectrum. Of these, only its tiny sliver of AWS-3 spectrum is actively supported by most existing cellphones.

Well, this paradigm changed in a fairly dramatic manner on Thursday, when SpaceX announced an agreement with Grain to acquire its "nationwide low-band spectrum license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band ."

Basically, under SpaceX's evolving plans, its space-based 2 GHz of mid-band spectrum will provide the backbone for a cellular network in the US, while this new 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band will ensure that Starlink Mobile signals are able to penetrate buildings. Also, with more smartphones expected to add support for SpaceX's existing terrestrial spectrum in 2027- 2028, Starlink Mobile will grow more competitive in the months ahead.

This brings us to the core of today's topic. According to a LinkedIn post penned by T-Mobile's CTO, John Saw, and titled ' Spectrum Alone Doesn't Make a Network ,' SpaceX's acquisition of a 14 megahertz sliver of the 800 MHz band is simply not enough:

"The Grain transaction involves approximately 14 MHz of spectrum that T-Mobile previously divested because it was no longer central to our network strategy. Even with this acquisition, Starlink Mobile would have roughly 80 MHz of spectrum, some of it uplink-only. Compare that to T-Mobile's nearly 400 MHz of mid-band and low-band spectrum holdings."

Taking a stab at the 2 GHz spectrum that SpaceX is positioning as the core of Starlink Mobile, T-Mobile's executive notes that "a satellite hundreds of kilometers above Earth faces approximately 50 dB more path loss than a terrestrial cell site just a kilometer away," and that "moving from 2 GHz to 800 MHz recovers only a few dB of that enormous disadvantage."

T-Mobile's CTO then adds:

"One satellite beam can cover an area served by hundreds of terrestrial cell sectors. Those terrestrial sectors provide the network density needed to support millions of customers streaming video, making calls, working, gaming, and using data simultaneously.

Covering a geographic area is one thing. Delivering the speed, responsiveness, and capacity customers expect from a modern 5G-Advanced network is another."

To be fair, SpaceX is working on establishing a complementary network of terrestrial cell towers, especially for its AWS-3 and AWS-4 spectrum. To that end, it is mulling innovative approaches, such as establishing small, low-power femtocell-type cellular base stations on existing Starlink dishes to avoid the massive upfront CapEx required for building cell towers.

On the flip side, the 800 MHz band does not propagate as well as the 600 MHz band . And, when T-Mobile launched its 5G network in 2019 with just 31 megahertz of the 600 MHz band , the service was widely panned for its sluggish speeds.

So, there you have it. While T-Mobile's CTO is on the point regarding the 800 MHz band's shortcomings, he is also being somewhat crafty by deliberately glossing over the fact that SpaceX intends to complement its network of Starlink satellites with terrestrial cell towers, including femtocell-type ones, which should allow the company to leverage its other spectrum holdings much more efficiently.

While Elon Musk might have exaggerated the implications around SpaceX's acquisition of a sliver of the 800 MHz spectrum, the fact that T-Mobile's CTO is now having to pen dedicated posts on LinkedIn to counter Musk's assertions clearly illustrates deep-seated unease within the so-called Big Three telecom players.

item.title: Intel Wants To Become The Go-To Foundry For ASICs And Specialized Chips, And Lip-Bu Tan’s Secret Weapon Is A Former Marvell Exec
item.description:
Intel is currently in the process of shedding its notoriously labyrinthine bureaucratic layers and the attendant inertia, while eyeing new markets and product categories for its fledgling advanced fabrication nodes, with the scorching-hot ASIC market serving as one such high-probability gambit on the part of the chipmaker's new CEO, Lip-Bu Tan.

As evidence, look no further than Intel's hiring of Dean Jarnac, a former Marvell executive, who has likely been tasked with furthering just such a goal, according to the tech analyst, Jack Gold.

Lip-Bu Tan broke years of internal precedents by a hiring a number of outsiders to lead Intel's key business segments, with Dean Jarnac's induction serving as a harbinger of sorts for Intel's pivot towards ASICs

The ASIC market has become quite crowded over the past few years. After all, we now have the TPUs that Google designs with Broadcom, Marvell, and MediaTek , the Trainium chips that Amazon designs in collaboration with Marvell, and the Maia AI accelerators that Microsoft designs with OpenAI, Marvell, and Broadcom. As if this were not enough, OpenAI recently collaborated with Broadcom to unveil a bespoke accelerator, dubbed Jalapeno , and Anthropic is reportedly developing an ASIC in collaboration with Broadcom and Samsung .

It is only natural, therefore, for Intel to try to capture a slice of this oven-hot pie. And, its biggest weapon so far for making just such an inroad is Dean Jarnac, a former Marvell executive who brings extensive ASIC-related experience to the proverbial table.

According to the tech analyst Jack Gold, Intel wants to leverage Jarnac's experience to clinch some much-needed contracts , which can then establish Intel's ASIC line on a firmer footing:

"[Marvell] designs chips, and so he knows, I’m assuming pretty well, how that whole process works when you work [for a] chip design company versus a company that designs and makes their own chips [like Intel]."

And, Intel has already had some success in its new pivot. As a case in point, back in July, the company announced a deal to design and manufacture Fortinet’s next-generation security processor for high-performance firewalls and security infrastructure. Even so, Intel's ambitions appear much more expansive, with its CFO, David Zinsner, noting in July that the company's ASIC business was approaching a $2 billion annual run rate, and could reach $4 billion "in the not-too-distant future."

Of course, Lip-Bu Tan's hiring of Jarnac is a part of a broader pattern, where Intel's new CEO is deliberately eschewing convention to position experienced outsiders within key areas of focus. By doing so, Tan appears to be striking a blow against Intel's entrenched bureaucracy, which has long become accustomed to internal promotions for key positions.

Elsewhere, we reported just today that NVIDIA might adopt Intel's Foveros packaging technology in 2028, which should act as a significant tailwind for the chipmaker. For the benefit of those who might not be aware, Foveros brings true 3D active-die stacking - face-to-face or face-to-back stacking directly over a base die/interposer - to the proverbial table, replete with very high interconnect density and extremely low signal latency due to short vertical paths offered by copper-to-copper hybrid bonding.

Foveros is a significant step-up from EMIB-T. As a refresher, Intel's EMIB connects multiple silicon chips (chiplets) inside a single processor package using tiny silicon "bridges" embedded directly inside the organic substrate, with high-density micro-bumps placed only at the edges where the chiplets meet the bridge.

The EMIB-T takes this approach a step further by sporting Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) drilled directly through the embedded silicon bridges. These vertical routing channels allow power and high-speed signals to flow straight up from the bottom of the chip package, through the bridge, and directly into the processors or memory sitting on top, enabling 3D stacking.

As if this were not enough, Intel has also been making silent inroads in the memory segment, working on upcoming technologies such as XBM and Z-Angle Memory (ZAM) . As a refresher, ZAM is a 3D-stacked DRAM where diagonal interconnects replace vertical through-silicon vias (TSVs), forming a central thermal pillar that better dissipates heat. It also leverages copper-to-copper hybrid bonding and eschews capacitors for greater density. In fact, Intel specifically highlighted its hiring of SK hynix's former CEO, Shou-Chi Lee , at its last earnings call while discussing its memory-related ambitions.

item.title: Acer Googlebook 14 Owner Stuck Cycling Between Acer Logo And “Updating” Screen For An Hour After Setup Update

item.title: Gears of War: E-Day Was Undercut by Game Pass, Says Alinea’s Rhys Elliott, as 722K Early Buyers Paid Just $30
item.description:
The first data on Gears of War: E-Day sales is out, and it's not looking good at all for Vancouver-based developer The Coalition . The studio was already reported to be very worried they'd be next in line for the chopping block after the second chapter of Xbox's Big Reset , which moved Halo, World's Edge, and Rare under Activision and laid off many employees across the division.

Now, Alinea Analytics reports that the game has sold only 230K units across Xbox (console and PC app) and Steam, a meager result for a triple-A game that has been in development for many years with a massive budget. 168K units were sold on Steam, and only 62K on Xbox . Revenue-wise, things are actually a bit better than the unit sales figure would suggest, with Alinea reporting $37 million earned, and the Xbox platform brought home $26 million of that slice.

How is it possible, given the much lower sales? Because of Game Pass , of course. The data shows 1.7 million players accessing Gears of War: E-Day via Game Pass, and 722K of those actually spent $30 for the Premium Edition Game Pass upgrade , which allowed them to access the game on October 1 instead of October 6.

Alinea's Rhys Elliott points to Game Pass as the main culprit: if those 722K subscribers who paid $30 to unlock the game early had instead been forced to purchase the full game, they would have generated nearly $40 million in revenue, rather than $21.7 million.

There's no doubt that Game Pass has proven to be an utter failure (save for edge cases, like State of Decay ) for Xbox, which is why even CEO Asha Sharma has now admitted that the subscription service caused a "free fall" in the division's balance sheet. The future of Xbox's biggest first-party titles, as evidenced by Call of Duty (Modern Warfare 4 won't be on Game Pass), is definitely out of the subscription service for their first year or so after release.

But that's only part of the Gears of War issue, I think. Despite E-Day's strong average review scores (although I didn't love it , and the average Steam score of 72% shows that the biggest PC community isn't excited for it, either), even if all those 722K turned into full-paying customers, the game still wouldn't have reached one million units sold yet .

This year alone, games like The Blood of Dawnwalker, Onimusha: Way of the Sword , PRAGMATA , Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve , and WARDOGS became million sellers way faster, and it's fair to assume their budgets were much less onerous, too. Back in June, insider Tom Henderson claimed that, according to his sources, the budget of Gears of War: E-Day was over $400 million . This remains unconfirmed, but even if it were just half of that, the game would have a very hard time recouping costs , let alone making a profit.

With several hundred employees left to cut from the 3,200 milestone set by Asha Sharma , The Coalition's future has never been so uncertain. The series itself might survive the studio, though, as shown just recently with 343 Industries/Halo Studios; besides, there's a Gears of War film adaptation directed by David Leitch on the way, and Xbox has just established th e XP division dedicated to transmedia efforts. The saga originally created by Epic Games certainly has the potential to do well on the big (or small) screen, which might help keep it relevant in Microsoft's eyes.

item.title: MSI Imported An RTX 5090 Unit For A Customer As A Replacement After It Stopped Working; Says AI Software Was The Culprit But Still Went The Extra Mile
item.description:
An RTX 5090 found inside an MSI pre-built gaming PC stopped working for one user when he powered it on one day, only to realize that it wasn’t being displayed on the AI software being run. Fearing the worst, the owner set up an RMA with the company, which was kind enough to import a replacement, but also stated that the GPU stopped working because of the very software being used.

RTX 5090 temperatures were completely fine when running a 27B AI model in Ollama

Typically, a fried or misused RTX 5090 has a tough time finding a replacement, because it was in the user’s possession and they are fully responsible for it, assuming they didn’t purchase a defective one. Secondly, given how scarce these GPUs are, companies are refusing to set up RMA tickets because they aren’t able to provide these replacements. Fortunately, for Reddit “u/crystalshower,” MSI had him covered.

What’s surprising to learn is that some companies will deny warranty for a burned RTX 5090 if you don’t use a “company approved” 12VHPWR power cable or adapter , and here we have MSI who has allegedly provided royal customer service to one of its customers by importing NVIDIA’s top-end GPU from Taiwan because they didn’t have any available units left in stock. What’s also surprising is that MSI informed the user that AI software was the reason why the RTX 5090 burned out.

After all, the chip’s temperature was in the 30°C - 50°C range when running a 4-bit quantized version of Qwen3.8-27B, leaving out the 12VHPWR power cable or connector as the only culprits.

Sadly, the Redditor hasn’t shared any pictures, so it’s difficult to verify these claims. As for whether MSI’s statement is hot air or not, when the RTX 5090 owner questioned the company about which specific software they believed was responsible for this accident, the customer care department didn’t reply. item.title: Circana’s Mat Piscatella Warns US Console Market Is Most Precarious Since Early 1980s, As Xbox Hardware Units Crash 33%
item.description:
The US console market is in real trouble , at least according to Circana's Mat Piscatella , who reckons it hasn't been this precarious since the early 1980s . In his breakdown of August's US sales data, the analyst revealed that year-to-date hardware unit sales through August have fallen 33% for Xbox and 25% for PlayStation compared to the same period last year. That puts Xbox at an all-time low in the US , while PlayStation has reached its lowest point since 2013 .

There's no big mystery here. In 2026 so far, the average price paid for a new Xbox console in the US is $529 , up 26% from a year ago, while the average price for a new PlayStation console is $597 , up 20%. Both figures are all-time US highs ; as Piscatella put it bluntly, price sensitivity is becoming a real problem.

August's numbers show the same pattern, as total hardware unit sales fell 15% year-over-year to 559K units, the lowest for any August since 2013 . PlayStation hardware units dropped 11%, to the platform’s lowest August since 2013, and Xbox units plunged 31%, its lowest August since 2020. Even Nintendo hardware unit sales dipped by 15%. Meanwhile, the average price paid for new hardware hit an August record of $541 , up from $476 a year ago.

That's how PlayStation 5 hardware dollar sales grew 17% in August, even as PlayStation unit sales fell: consumers are buying fewer consoles but paying considerably more per console. In case you were wondering, Nintendo Switch 2 led the US market in both units and dollars for both August and year-to-date , with PlayStation 5 second across the board and Xbox Series S|X a distant third. Many of these issues trace back to the crazy component costs . Sony's April price increase , which raised the PlayStation 5 and Digital Edition by $100 each and the PS5 Pro by $150 to $899.99, was driven by soaring memory prices as manufacturers prioritized demand from AI data centers , and Xbox and Nintendo are suffering in the same way.

Piscatella sees one potential bright spot on the horizon, noting that the release of the Big Video Game in November may help ease some of these declines. He doesn't name it, but there's little doubt he is referring to Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI , which launches on November 19 . Even that comes with caveats, though. Any GTA VI bump inevitably depends on product availability, given the ongoing RAM and component crisis, and on pricing. We have already seen new PS5 Pro stock drying up ahead of the launch, to the point that GameStop now prices used consoles well above new ones .

The broader picture wasn't much brighter. Overall, US video game spending fell 9% in August to $4.3 billion , driven primarily by an 18% drop in mobile, while console content spending declined 7%. PC content was a rare bright spot, rising by 13%.

Piscatella also provided an updated year-to-date Top 10 chart of the best-selling premium games released in 2026. CAPCOM's Resident Evil: Requiem is still on top , although we all know the throne of this particular chart will soon be conquered by the aforementioned Big Video Game.

item.title: Pearl Abyss Blames Review Process For Crimson Desert’s 77 Metacritic, Yet 6 Million Sales Disagree
item.description:
By every metric, Pearl Abyss ' Crimson Desert is a smashing success. Having sold over 6 million copies and generating $427 million in revenue, the Korean developer proved not only that it was more than ready to handle a sprawling single-player open-world game, but also that a development approach that takes player feedback into heavy consideration is the key to success. This is made even more impressive by the fact that the game didn't score well in launch reviews, an issue that European CEO Lybee Park pins on both the nature of the review process and the game itself.

"Critics had to play the build that is not the exact same version as the launch game," said European CEO Lybee Park on The Game Business Show . "They also had limited time. Usually, the classical approach when they review the game is to follow the main storyline. But our unique charm is spread across our in-game world. All those tiny details that are hidden. I am not sure critics had the fair chance to explore those during the review period."

Having reviewed Crimson Desert , I can confirm that Pearl Abyss did its very best to give us as much time as possible to explore Pywel and experience a lot of what it has to offer besides the main story, although the roughness of early builds led to some frustration, including inventory space that was even more limited than it was in the launch build.

Unfortunately, the game is so massive that even after hundreds of hours, it is possible to discover all sorts of secrets, so once I realized this, I decided to stop rushing the main story and immerse myself in this world. This is probably the reason why I scored it 9.0 in a late review as opposed to other critics, a score I would now increase with the significant improvements introduced for the story in the Enhanced upgrade. After all, a regular player isn't gonna rush through a game like this, so slowing down let me align my perspective with most players'.

Still, this lukewarm reception didn't prevent Pearl Abyss from achieving a dream of sorts for their game: excellent console sales. "Console is the dream goal. The Korean game industry is known for PC. It’s more familiar to us," said Park. "But people have been growing up playing and watching those amazing console titles, and dreamed of making one. So those experiences making PC games has now given us more chance to understand console market, console language and console fans’ needs and wants."

Considering the ongoing support Crimson Desert is receiving from Pearl Abyss , but also from modders, which will culminate in a few weeks with the Charting the Unknown DLC expansion, I have little doubt the game will become even more successful. A success that I believe is wholly deserved: while the game is not terribly original, its incredible combat system and the sum of its parts, now properly connected by a solid narrative, more than make up for it.

item.title: Sony’s PlayStation 5 QSSR May Lack the Shortcut That Made PSSR Easy, As Older Games Could Need a Later SDK
item.description:
Last week, Sony revealed the Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) upscaler for PlayStation 5 , an AI-driven image upscaling technology not dissimilar to the PlayStation 5 Pro 's PSSR upscaler that can be used on the base system to bridge the image quality gap with the mid-generation refresh. According to Daniel Craig, Principal Engineer for Graphics R&D at SIE , retrofits will be easy and require only a bit of tuning , but there could be development challenges that significantly limit how many older games will support the new upscaler.

"One thing we need to keep in mind is the status of QSSR within the SDK framework on the Sony development platform," Digital Foundry 's Richard Leadbetter said in a recent Q&A video shared on YouTube . "Is it available for older versions of the SDK? And if not, then that does present problems for retrofits, right? Because the developer would need to update their older games to run on the later SDK."

"I did hear over the weekend that might be a bit of a challenge for older titles," he continued. This wasn't the case for PSSR , as it was possible to add the upscaler to games running on older SDKs, making it much easier and potentially more cost-effective for developers. For this reason, a centralized toggle is also not possible, as there is no sort of centralized library as there was with PSSR that enabled it.

If an SDK update would be required to retrofit older PlayStation 5 games with the QSSR upscaler, I can honestly see only the biggest games getting support. While doing this update may sound easy to the uninitiated, it is a demanding process that requires weeks of porting work and quality assurance, which may not be worth it for a single-player game that has been released, say, three to four years ago, and that is not enjoying particularly long legs on the market.

Even if QSSR will not be retrofitted in many games, there's no denying that it is an exciting development for the base PlayStation 5 , as too many games launch with average image quality, which upscalers like AMD FSR can't always clean up at higher output resolutions like 1440p and 4K. In addition, with what many believe will be the longest cross-generation period of all time, QSSR will ensure that games also targeting the PlayStation 6 will not leave too much to be desired in terms of visual quality on the base system.

item.title: HelixSR Mod Brings DLSS 3.7 to the Steam Deck and AMD Handhelds, Running Faster Than FSR 4 in Early Tests
item.description:
A new mod is giving the Steam Deck and other AMD -powered handhelds something they were never supposed to have: NVIDIA's DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sampling) upscaling.

HelixSR , released two days ago on GitHub by developer lonewolf0622 , is a drop-in replacement for AMD's FSR 3.1 upscaler on Direct3D 12 that runs NVIDIA's DLSS neural network on AMD GPUs instead. Specifically, it uses Preset E (which the developer calls Model E), introduced with DLSS 3.7 , the final iteration of DLSS's CNN-based model before NVIDIA switched to Transformer models with DLSS 4. That's actually a great fit for handhelds, since the CNN model is considerably lighter to run . Games still think they are talking to FSR 3.1, but what actually comes out is DLSS's reconstruction. The trick is that the network runs as plain DirectX 12 compute shaders , so it needs no NVIDIA driver, no CUDA, and no ROCm, and it even works on Linux through Proton and vkd3d-proton.

AMD's own machine learning upscaler, FSR 4, is officially limited to RDNA 4 GPUs , leaving the Steam Deck's RDNA 2 chip and even RDNA 3 -based handhelds like the ROG Ally X stuck with the older, visibly inferior FSR 3 , which still relies on temporal upscaling. Community workarounds can get FSR 4 running on those devices, but at a steep performance cost that the handheld machines simply cannot handle with taxing games.

That’s where HelixSR comes in. One ResetEra user measured roughly 3.5 ms per frame for HelixSR at 800p, versus 4.5 ms for FSR 4, and 7 ms versus 11 ms at 1080p, with the Steam Deck's GPU running at 1400 MHz. On the BC-250, the original poster saw an even starker difference when running IO Interactive's Hitman: World of Assassination at 4K, with 35 FPS using the DLSS Quality preset against 17 FPS with FSR 4.

Opinions on image quality vary a bit. The original poster found it not quite as good as FSR 4, but still much better than FSR 3. YouTuber BlackHeart909 was more enthusiastic, suggesting it might even look better than FSR 4 in some instances . In their testing, BlackHeart909 hit 34 to 40 FPS in Pragmata on the Steam Deck in Performance mode, and 35 to 40 FPS in CONTROL Resonant on the ROG Ally X at 1080p, a game that had previously suffered from heavy ghosting. Dropping the Ally X's output to 720p allowed a locked 60 FPS. They did have to patch the mod to get it running on the Ally X, though, and said they'll pass the fixes on to the developer of HelixSR.

HelixSR is evolving very quickly. In the few days since its release, the developer has pushed out five updates , adding a single-file installer, a new Quality Super-Sampled Mode (QSSM) that renders above screen resolution for cleaner edges, and a fix for the blurry image reported on RDNA 3 GPUs under Windows, the same issue that affected BlackHeart909's ROG Ally X. It still has limits, though: it supports Direct3D 12 games only, with no Vulkan support, and games that don't use FSR 3.1 require OptiScaler .

For Steam Deck owners who have watched the upscaling gap widen over the past couple of years, though, it is a very intriguing development that might well prolong the device's longevity while Valve waits for the perfect time to introduce a Steam Deck 2 device. Last we heard from AMD leaker Kepler_L2 , Valve is targeting 2028 , although the ongoing component crisis could delay its release.

item.title: TSMC’s Upcoming Earnings Might Provide Major Clues For AI & Overall Chip Price Hikes, Believes Analyst — Elon Musk’s Terafab Might Surface As Well
item.description:
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSMC) upcoming earnings call on the 15th can provide additional details about the firm's potential partnership with Elon Musk's Terafab project. A potential TSMC and Musk cooperation gained headlines last week after the Tesla executive confirmed that he was in discussions with the firm for such a project. However, Musk later asserted that any such cooperation would at best enable TSMC to sublease a portion of his planned massive chip production project.

TSMC's A14 Progress, Capital Expenditure & Global Expansion Among Key Factors To Observe In Upcoming Earnings, Says Analyst

With all indicators pointing towards smooth progress at Intel for its 14A chip manufacturing process technology, all eyes are on TSMC's A14 technology. The A14 process is the marketing equivalent of the 14A node, and TSMC's official estimates continue to suggest that the process will enter volume production in 2028.

However, unconfirmed supply chain reports from Taiwan have made some rather bold claims for TSMC's next-generation chip technology. For instance, a rather interesting report that surfaced in early September claimed that the firm could enter early stage production with the process technology in April 2027 and kick off mass production in the year's latter half .

Now, as TSMC gears up to report its third quarter earnings next week, analyst Chen Huiming at the Hong Kong based Juxin Capital believes that TSMC's progress with the A14 node will be one of several factors to watch out for.

Apart from the technology, the analyst outlines that TSMC's capital expenditure will be a key figure to watch since it will indicate its expectations about future AI demand. As the largest contract chip production company in the world, TSMC has significant visibility into the projections of firms such as NVIDIA and can adjust its production spending accordingly.

Additionally, Huiming outlined that TSMC's comments about the CoWoS packaging technology will be interesting. CoWoS is the top AI chip packaging technology in the world and offers superior performance for high performance chips. However, for products designed with power efficiency in mind, Intel's E MIB-T is reportedly shaping up to be a contender .

Finally, the analyst added that with rumors floating around that TSMC might increase prices next year and its CFO not having ruled out such a possibility, any shifts in its gross margin guidance could help determine whether the firm has any such plans. As for the Terafab deal, the fact that TSMC chooses to formally address the issue should be interesting.

Apple might have wanted to believe that incorporating a swath of upgrades on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max could help it to avoid a sales slump caused by soaring DRAM chip prices , but even a trillion-dollar giant isn’t immune to its effects. According to the latest report, the company has asked suppliers to cut production by 15-20 percent, as low demand for its latest flagships forces it to make some hard choices.

Despite being slightly more expensive than its immediate predecessors, the iPhone 18 Pro cannot command a higher shipment tally, at least for now

A fresh update from Nikkei Asia talks about Apple reaching out to various suppliers and requesting them to cut iPhone 18 Pro production by up to 20 percent. The cut varies by supplier, with the report noting that the Cupertino firm has been slightly more conservative with shipments since early September. Two component manufacturers have claimed that, for October, orders have been slashed by at least 15 percent compared to the original order.

On the bright side, not all suppliers are affected, but there’s growing uncertainty in Apple’s supply chain, as there’s no confirmation on whether the iPhone maker will maintain that conservative approach during a sales slump. Typically, when newer iPhone models launch, there’s a massive spike in pre-orders, with Apple’s suppliers expected to boost production, but the complete opposite is happening here. However, we don’t entirely believe that the DRAM shortage is responsible for this outcome.

As the majority of you know, Apple hasn’t introduced a base iPhone 18 or iPhone Air 2 this year, and with the iPhone 18 Pro starting from $1,199 for the 256GB model, consumers would naturally feel that it wasn’t worth the money to switch. The latest flagship is $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro, and the lack of a less expensive option means customers have few alternatives other than sticking with their current device.

It’s possible that the situation changes early next year, when Apple is expected to announce the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2. The base model is said to arrive with the regular A20, which will be significantly downgraded compared to the A20 Pro , but as long as Apple can target a competitive starting price, its popularity could surpass the iPhone 17.

item.title: A Medical Emergency Forced A User To Downgrade From Windows 11 26H2 To Windows 10, But The Matter Is Being Blown Way Out Of Proportion
item.description:
No operating system is perfect, and in the case of Windows 11, you have to deal with more quirks than you’d like, despite Microsoft’s promise that it’ll continue to optimize the platform. In the case of one user, version 26H2 became the reason why he downgraded to Windows 10, but the medical reason mentioned for the switch has been overblown.

Windows language input method took 20 minutes to finish while the user was searching for his family member’s affliction

After recently installing Windows 11 26H2 on his computer, Redditor “u/Shanaudio” had to rush a family member to the hospital over a medical emergency. After the situation de-escalated, the user returned home and decided to look up more details on his family member’s affliction. Unfortunately, because the 26H2 update was installed just a few hours prior, there were some roadblocks in the way.

To search online for the medical condition, it was important to install the built-in Windows language input method, and it took a full 20 minutes to finish. The Redditor states that on Windows 10, the total time required elapsed only 2 minutes, forcing him to downgrade to Microsoft’s older operating system. While it’s thoughtful that the user is trying to learn more about this family member’s condition, searching online is a recipe for disaster.

Google’s search results are tremendously skewed when it comes to health-related information, which could result in more harm and unnecessary worry. Additionally, what’s stopping the user from searching for the same medical condition on his phone? We understand that everyone has preferences, but not to the extent that you cannot go through a phone and search for relevant information.

There are also dedicated apps for services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude to seek advice, but again, that’s a terrible idea, and we recommend seeking professional medical advice. In short, while we can sympathize with having to wait a good 20 minutes for the update to be installed, that’s no reason to downgrade. Instead, you can simply disable Windows 11 updates and be free from this headache altogether.

We rarely check for updates, keeping the service completely disabled, so for anyone dealing with similar problems on Windows 11, we advise following a similar approach.
